title: DAVID’S DEATHBED AND THE YOUNG WOMAN BESIDE HIM: The Strange Story of Abishag
paragraphs: DAVID’S DEATHBED AND THE YOUNG WOMAN BESIDE HIM: The Strange Story of Abishag

She entered Scripture beside a dying king, barely spoke in the recorded story, and somehow became connected to a struggle for Israel’s throne. But hidden inside this strange account is something far bigger than Abishag, David, or Solomon: a haunting picture of fading human glory—and our desperate need for the King whose throne will never grow cold.
There is a young woman standing beside the bed of one of the most famous men in the Bible.
She is beautiful.
He is dying.
And almost nobody talks about her.
The old man beneath the blankets is David.
David.
The shepherd boy who faced Goliath.
The fugitive who survived Saul.
The warrior who united a kingdom.
The poet who sang, “The LORD is my shepherd.”
The king whose name would become inseparable from Israel’s hope for the Messiah.
But when 1 Kings opens, we do not meet David holding a sword.
We meet him beneath blankets.
And he cannot get warm.
That detail should stop us.
Because Scripture has a way of stripping human glory down to the truth.
The Hebrew says:
“וְהַמֶּלֶךְ דָּוִד זָקֵן, בָּא בַּיָּמִים”
Vehammelekh David zaqen, ba bayyamim.
“King David was old, advanced in days.”
Then comes the painful sentence:
“וְלֹא יִחַם לוֹ”
Velo yicham lo.
He could not get warm.
The man who once made armies tremble could not command warmth into his own body.
The man who had survived lions, bears, giants, spears, rebellions, betrayal, warfare, grief, scandal, and consequences was now losing a battle every human being eventually loses.
Time.
No title could stop it.
No palace could stop it.
No army could stop it.
No reputation could stop it.
David was still king.
But David was dying.
And maybe that is where this story begins speaking directly to us.
Because we spend so much of life trying to become something.
Successful.
Admired.
Secure.
Beautiful.
Influential.
Comfortable.
Remembered.
We build names people will recognize and lives people will envy.
Then Scripture quietly walks us into David’s bedroom and whispers:
Look again.
This is where earthly glory eventually goes.
The crown remains.
The body weakens.
The achievements remain.
The heartbeat slows.
People may still call you important while your lungs are taking their final breaths.
And suddenly the questions that consumed your life become embarrassingly small beside the question that actually matters:
Who are you before God?
David’s servants proposed an unusual solution. They would search for a young virgin who could attend the king, lie close to him, and provide warmth.
They searched throughout Israel.
And they found her.
Abishag.
“אֲבִישַׁג הַשּׁוּנַמִּית”
Avishag ha-Shunammit.
Abishag the Shunammite.
She came from Shunem, and Scripture emphasizes something immediately about her.
She was extraordinarily beautiful.
But read carefully.
Because this is where careless retellings can turn Scripture into something Scripture never says.
Abishag was brought to David as an attendant and caregiver. The Hebrew describes her as a sokhenet—an attendant or one caring closely for the king—and says she ministered to him.
Then the biblical writer deliberately adds:
Vehammelekh lo yeda‘ah.
Literally:
“The king did not know her.”
In biblical Hebrew, “know” can function as a discreet expression for sexual relations, and that is clearly the meaning here.
David did not have sexual relations with Abishag.
That matters.
The text wants us to know it.
Abishag shared proximity to the king without becoming another sexual conquest.
And the contrast with an earlier chapter in David’s life is difficult to miss, even though Scripture does not explicitly tell us to equate the two scenes.
Years earlier, David had been in royal comfort when he saw another beautiful woman.
Bathsheba.
That encounter became one of the darkest scandals of his life.
Adultery.
Deception.
Uriah’s death.
Nathan’s confrontation.
Consequences that tore through David’s household.
David eventually confessed his sin, and God forgave him—but forgiveness did not magically erase every earthly consequence.
Now, near the end of his life, another beautiful woman is near his bed.
But this time Scripture explicitly says:
He did not know her.
Do not misunderstand that.
The Bible is not presenting David’s old age as though one final act of restraint somehow paid for Bathsheba.
David could never undo his own sin.
Neither can we.
That is exactly why grace is grace.
You cannot go backward and become the person who never sinned.
You cannot climb into yesterday and unsay the words.
You cannot reopen the moment before the affair.
Before the addiction.
Before the betrayal.
Before the secret.
Before the compromise.
Before you became the person you promised yourself you would never become.
Some of you reading this know exactly what that feels like.
You love Jesus now.
But there are memories you wish had never happened.
People may know the cleaned-up version of you.
God knows the whole story.
The private browser history.
The message you deleted.
The person you used.
The lie you protected.
The bitterness you fed.
The marriage you damaged.
The years you wasted.
The faith you performed publicly while starving privately.
And sometimes the enemy takes those memories and whispers:
“That is who you really are.”
But David’s story refuses both cheap excuses and hopeless condemnation.
Sin matters.
Consequences matter.
Repentance matters.
Grace matters.
David was not saved because David managed to become impressive again.
David needed mercy.
Just like us.
And that is where the story begins turning toward Someone greater than David.
But first, the room around the dying king becomes dangerous.
While David grows weak, one of his sons sees opportunity.
Adonijah.
Scripture says:
“וַאֲדֹנִיָּה בֶן־חַגִּית מִתְנַשֵּׂא לֵאמֹר אֲנִי אֶמְלֹךְ”
Adonijah exalted himself, saying:
“I will be king.”
Notice the heart of rebellion.
“I will.”
God had His purposes.
David had not yet died.
Solomon was the son David would publicly designate to succeed him.
But Adonijah was already reaching for the throne.
And Scripture gives us a painful detail about David’s parenting: his father had not confronted him by asking why he behaved as he did.
That single observation should make every parent uncomfortable.
Because sometimes love becomes distorted into avoiding necessary confrontation.
Sometimes we call something “grace” when we are actually afraid to speak truth.
Sometimes we protect people from discomfort until they become strangers to correction.
Adonijah wanted a crown.
He gathered chariots.
Horsemen.
Fifty men running before him.
He built the appearance of kingship before possessing the authority of kingship.
And human beings are still doing this.
We want the appearance.
The platform.
The applause.
The relationship.
The ministry.
The recognition.
The title.
The influence.
We want to look chosen.
But there is a terrifying difference between what you can manufacture and what God has actually given you.
Adonijah could organize a procession.
He could not manufacture God’s appointment.
Eventually David acted.
Solomon was publicly installed as king.
Adonijah’s attempted seizure collapsed.
And for a moment, it seemed the crisis had passed.
But Abishag’s story was not finished.
After David died, Adonijah approached Bathsheba.
He asked her for something that sounded almost strangely modest.
He wanted Abishag.
“Give me Abishag the Shunammite as my wife.”
Just one woman.
That was all.
Or was it?
Bathsheba carried the request to Solomon.
And Solomon immediately recognized enormous political implications in it.
His response is explosive.
In Hebrew:
“וְלָמָה אַתְּ שֹׁאֶלֶת אֶת־אֲבִישַׁג הַשֻּׁנַמִּית לַאֲדֹנִיָּהוּ וְשַׁאֲלִי־לוֹ אֶת־הַמְּלוּכָה”
“Why do you ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? Ask for him the kingdom also.”
Read that again.
Ask for Abishag?
You might as well ask for the kingdom.

Whatever Adonijah may personally have intended, Solomon understood the request as bound up with a renewed claim to royal power. In the world of ancient monarchy, relationships involving women associated with a former king could carry dynastic significance. More importantly, we do not have to guess how Solomon interpreted this particular request—the biblical text tells us.
To Solomon, Abishag was not merely a beautiful young woman someone wanted to marry.
The request touched the throne.
And suddenly the young woman who entered the story to warm an old man’s body stands near the center of a deadly struggle over kingship.
Think about Abishag for a moment.
Not as a symbol.
As a human being.
Scripture tells us very little about her inner life.
We are never given a recorded speech from her.
We are not told what she thought when royal servants arrived.
We are not told how she felt entering David’s chambers.
We are not told whether she was frightened.
Honored.
Confused.
Overwhelmed.
We are not told what she thought when David died.
We are not told what she thought when Adonijah asked for her.
And that silence should make us careful.
We should not invent emotions and call them Scripture.
But perhaps the silence itself reminds us of something painfully human.
Some people appear in other people’s stories while carrying stories nobody asks them to tell.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Everybody remembers what happened around you.
Few people ask what happened inside you.
You were the child in the divorce.
The spouse beside the addiction.
The person abandoned after somebody else made the decision.
The believer quietly holding the family together.
The woman whose pain became somebody else’s gossip.
The man everyone thought was strong because nobody saw him collapse.
You served.
You stayed.
You carried things.
You watched powerful personalities make decisions that changed your life.
And somehow your name became attached to a story you never asked to enter.
God sees people whose voices human history barely records.
Abishag may occupy only a small amount of biblical space.
But God knew her completely.
And He knows you.
Still, there is an even deeper ache running through this chapter.
David is dying.
Adonijah wants the throne.
Solomon receives the throne.
People maneuver around power.
And eventually Solomon will die too.
Every human king dies.
Every earthly throne eventually belongs to someone else.
Every empire becomes history.
Every celebrity becomes an old photograph.
Every billionaire eventually leaves every dollar behind.
Every body praised for its beauty returns to dust.
Every hand gripping power eventually opens.
David could not remain king forever.
Solomon could not remain king forever.
Israel needed something no ordinary son of David could finally provide.
A King death could not keep.
And centuries later, another Son of David came.
Jesus Christ.
This is where the Bible’s larger story becomes breathtaking.
Jesus is repeatedly identified in the New Testament with David’s royal line and messianic hope.
But Jesus did what David never could.
David defeated Goliath.
Jesus defeated the greater enemies—sin and death.
David ruled Jerusalem.
Jesus announced the kingdom of God.
David committed grievous sin and needed forgiveness.
Jesus was without sin and became the sacrifice through whom sinners receive forgiveness.
David eventually lay beneath blankets unable to keep himself warm.
Jesus willingly went to a cross.
David entered the grave and remained there.
Jesus entered the grave and rose.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of sinful people successfully repairing themselves.
It is the announcement that God came to rescue sinners who could not rescue themselves.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe beneath everything people see, you are tired.
Tired of managing appearances.
Tired of promising God you will change and returning to the same chains.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of carrying shame into worship.
Tired of knowing Bible verses while secretly wondering whether Jesus could still want someone who has done what you have done.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
It says Christ is sufficient.
Repentance is not pretending the darkness never happened.
Repentance turns from sin toward God.
Grace is not God announcing that holiness no longer matters.
Grace is God giving guilty people what they could never earn through Jesus Christ.
The cross does not minimize your sin.
The cross reveals how deadly sin is.
And then it reveals how far God was willing to go to save sinners.
David knew something about this.
After his sin was exposed, Psalm 51 records the cry of a man who could no longer hide behind a crown:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
That is not the prayer of a man polishing his reputation.
That is the prayer of someone who knows he needs God to do what he cannot do for himself.
Maybe that needs to become your prayer tonight.
Not:
“God, make me look better.”
Not:
“God, make everybody forget.”
Not:
“God, protect my reputation.”
But:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
“Clean me.”
“Change me.”
“I am tired of hiding.”
Sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we spent years building.
And please hear this too:
Do not turn Abishag into gossip.
Do not turn David’s weakness into entertainment.
Do not turn Adonijah’s ambition into merely another strange Bible story.
Let the text turn the mirror toward us.
Because somewhere inside these chapters, most of us recognize ourselves.
We know what it is to want what God has not given.
We know what it is to manufacture appearances.
We know what it is to carry consequences.
We know what it is to grow tired.
We know what it is to need mercy.
And every one of us is moving toward the same unavoidable appointment David faced.
Death.
The question is not whether your body will eventually fail.
The question is whether you belong to the King who conquered the grave.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people behave better.
He came calling sinners to repentance, forgiving those who come to Him, reconciling us to God, and making His people new.
That is why the Gospel Warrior message will always return here:
Not because scandal becomes irrelevant.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because Christians should romanticize sin.
But because Jesus Christ can write redemption into lives human beings would have discarded.
Your worst chapter does not have authority over Christ.
Your shame does not sit on the throne.
Your addiction does not sit on the throne.
Your past does not sit on the throne.
Your critics do not sit on the throne.
Your success does not sit on the throne.
Jesus does.
If this article made you think of someone who has been running from God, share it with them.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves that you love Jesus. Salvation cannot be bought, and grace cannot be purchased.
Christ cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Eternal life cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So before you leave this story, picture that bedroom one final time.
David beneath the blankets.
Abishag beside him.
The palace whispering.
A son reaching for a crown.
Another son preparing to inherit it.
An old king breathing toward eternity.
Everything humans fight to possess slipping through human fingers.
Then look beyond Jerusalem.
Beyond David.
Beyond Solomon.
Beyond every earthly throne.
Look toward a hill outside Jerusalem where the true Son of David wore a crown made of thorns.
Look toward a sealed tomb that could not keep Him.
And understand the difference.
David needed someone beside him because he was dying.
Jesus came beside us because we were dying.
David could not hold onto his kingdom.
Jesus says His kingdom will never end.
David’s body grew cold.
Jesus walked out of the grave alive.
That is our hope.
Not that we lived without scandal.
Not that we never failed.
Not that our story remained clean enough to impress religious people.
Our hope is that sinners can repent, ruined people can be redeemed, guilty people can be forgiven, dead hearts can be made alive, and shattered stories can be placed into the hands of Jesus Christ.
But above everything else...
Come to Jesus.
Because one day every blanket will be useless.
Every title will disappear.
Every possession will belong to somebody else.
Every human throne will be empty.
And on that day, the only story that will finally matter is whether your story was surrendered to the King who walked out of His grave.
The crown eventually falls from every human head—but grace still belongs to the sinner who falls at the feet of Jesus.
